name: Inverse Rendering and Optical Properties

# Inverse Rendering and Optical Properties


## Overview
Inverse rendering and optical properties methods reconstruct physical scene parameters—such as volume density, extinction coefficients, albedo, or environmental illumination—from a set of observed images [S1, unofficial][S2, S3]. This family is distinguished from standard [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) by its explicit focus on recovering physically meaningful material properties (e.g., via adjoint derivatives or neural field residuals) rather than merely optimizing a black-box radiance field [S1, unofficial][S2, S3].

## Shared principles

## Subtopics

### [Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Tracing](1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md)
Optimizes a 3D volume density grid to match reference images using [differentiable path tracing](#21778-differentiable-path-tracing.md) [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings by explicitly optimizing physical volume parameters (grid-based extinction) using a differentiable path tracer rather than neural field representations [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md]. Choose this when you need to reconstruct complex volumetric properties from multiple viewpoints while maintaining physical accuracy through [path replay backpropagation](#6780-path-replay-backpropagation.md) [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md].

### [Neural Radiosity](6755-neural-radiosity.md)
Represents the outgoing radiance field as a neural network and optimizes its parameters by minimizing the residual of the rendering equation [6755-neural-radiosity.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings by treating the rendering equation as a self-supervised loss function, allowing direct optimization of scene properties without explicit light transport simulation per step [6755-neural-radiosity.md]. Choose this when you want to compute global illumination without relying on rasterizers or path tracers, and when viewpoint independence is desired [6755-neural-radiosity.md].

### [NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields)](10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md)
Reconstructs a 3D scene representation from images under unconstrained, known lighting, enabling view synthesis and relighting with indirect illumination [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings by using learned neural approximations for visibility and surface intersections to reduce the complexity of direct and indirect lighting calculations [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md]. Choose this when you need to support arbitrary [environment lighting](#17399-environment-map-as-image-based-lighting.md) and one-bounce global illumination, using a learned neural visibility field to reduce light transport simulation complexity [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md].

### [Inverse Rendering with Exponential Phase Function](18392-inverse-rendering-with-exponential-phase-function.md)
Estimates scattering parameters (extinction coefficient $\sigma_t$, scattering coefficient $\sigma_s$, and [phase function](#3111-phase-function.md) parameters $\Phi_p$) of a homogeneous translucent slab from captured images using a physics-based differentiable renderer [18392-inverse-rendering-with-exponential-phase-function.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings by focusing on analytical parameter estimation for specific slab geometries rather than general scene reconstruction [18392-inverse-rendering-with-exponential-phase-function.md]. Choose this for fitting complex scattering profiles where standard phase functions fail, specifically employing a three-degree [exponential phase function](#18395-exponential-phase-function.md) [18392-inverse-rendering-with-exponential-phase-function.md].

### Inverse Rendering with Adjoint Derivatives
An optimization method that estimates scene optical properties (position, scale, [rotation](#19376-rotation.md), cross-section, spherical harmonic coefficients) from images using gradient-based optimization with adjoint derivatives of the forward pass [S1, unofficial]. It starts optimization with a small number of primitives and gradually generates new primitives to add detail [S1, unofficial]. It uses a Bound Adam optimizer and an L1 error, D-SSIM, plus regularization loss function [S1, unofficial].

### Reflectance Fields
A 3D representation for inverse rendering where the scene is represented as a field of volume density, surface normals, and [Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Functions](#14809-bidirectional-reflectance-distribution-function-brdf.md) (BRDFs) [S2]. It augments [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) with an additional MLP to model lighting, models BRDFs with spherical Gaussians, incorporates SDF-based representation, and introduces regularization to stabilize normals from NeRF's foggy geometry [S2]. These methods suffer from extremely time-consuming optimization and slow rendering speed [S2].

### Light Reconstruction
Optimizes environmental illumination instead of volume properties to match desired volume appearance. Volume properties (emission, albedo, extinction) are assumed spatially varying but fixed during this optimization [S3].

## Background
The use of adjoint derivatives for volumetric inverse rendering was highlighted in work on volumetric ray-traced primitives, which allows for noiseless and efficient rendering of scattering media [S1, unofficial]. Reflectance fields, which model BRDFs and lighting via neural networks, have been surveyed as a key approach for inverse rendering, though they face challenges in optimization time and rendering speed [S2]. Light reconstruction, as an alternative to modifying volume properties, has been explored in the context of volume stylization, where environmental illumination is optimized to match desired appearances [S3].
